title: Salim, Mu'adh and the others
hookLine: four the Prophet ﷺ named as teachers of the Qur'an: Ibn Mas'ud, Salim, Mu'adh and Ubayy

cards: A short list. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, once named the people to go to if you wanted to learn the Qur'an: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Salim the freed man of Abu Hudhayfah, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Mu'adh ibn Jabal.

Three of those names have had a day of their own on this path already. One hasn't. And he's the one who, on paper, didn't belong: a man who had once been owned, whose name in the hadith is tied to someone else's.

teach.b: The hadith is in Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abdullah ibn Amr: learn the Qur'an from four.
Alongside the other three stands Salim, whose title is mawla, a word that here means a freed man still linked to the household that freed him. Tradition says Abu Hudhayfah took him in as a son.
In the hadith, his name doesn't stand alone. And the Prophet sent people to him anyway.

teach.h: HE LED THE PRAYER AT QUBA.
teach.b: Bukhari also records what happened at Quba, before the Prophet himself reached Medina. When the first emigrants arrived, Salim led them in prayer, and the report gives the reason: he knew the most Qur'an of them.
Not the best family. Not the most wealth. The most Qur'an.

So the men who had left Mecca stood behind a freed man, because of what he carried in his memory. The biographies, not Bukhari, add that Salim was later killed at the battle of Yamamah, carrying the emigrants' banner.
What the hadith gives for certain is the list, and the list is a kind of permission. It tells anyone who wants to learn: go to the ones who know, whoever they are.

teach.h: WHAT YOU CARRY, NOT YOUR NAME.
teach.b: And it tells anyone who teaches, whatever their past: what you carry matters more than the name you were given.

That closes a week of companions: Abu Ayyub the host, Sa'd and the throne, Uways and his mother, the Ansar women, Abu Musa's voice, Hudhayfah's questions, and now Salim at the front of the line in Quba.

how: Muslims learn to recite the Qur'an from a teacher face to face, and chains of recitation are traced back through companions such as Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy ibn Ka'b.

the one who knows the most Qur'an.

practice: Bring to mind whoever taught you to read the Qur'an, or taught you al-Fatiha, the prayer, or the first Arabic letters: a parent, a teacher at the mosque, a friend, an app voice, even.
If you never had one, think of whoever first taught you something you still use every day. Thank them in your mind, and if you pray, ask good for them.
